text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

text:
🚨MASSIVE: Russia Threatens Full-Scale Space War Against ELON MUSK, Puts all Starlink Satellites in the Crosshairs

Russia has issued increasingly sharp warnings over the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network in military operations against Russian territory. Moscow has suggested that if Starlink becomes directly involved in enabling deep strikes inside Russia, the satellites themselves could become targets.

The warning carries a far bigger implication than a dispute over internet connectivity.

Starlink has become deeply embedded in Ukraine’s wartime communications architecture, supporting battlefield communications, drone operations and the transmission of real-time information. As a result, Russia increasingly views the network not simply as civilian infrastructure, but as a strategic military enabler.

Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has warned that attempts to interfere with Russia’s satellite capabilities could trigger what he described as a full-scale space war, while Russian officials have repeatedly threatened retaliation against systems supporting military operations.

Starlink has demonstrated that commercial satellite networks can become strategic infrastructure during wartime. The same technology that provides internet connectivity to remote communities can also support drones, command networks, battlefield communications and intelligence operations.

And that creates a fundamental vulnerability: whoever controls the network can potentially influence access to it.

India Cannot Build Its Digital Future Around a Foreign Network

For India, the lesson is not that Starlink should be rejected. The lesson is that Starlink cannot become India's only strategic option.

India can benefit enormously from satellite broadband, particularly in remote villages, difficult terrain, islands and areas where conventional fibre infrastructure is expensive or difficult to deploy. Foreign companies can bring capital, technology and competition to the Indian market.

But strategic dependence is an entirely different matter.

If a network is controlled by a foreign company operating within another country's geopolitical ecosystem, India cannot assume that access will remain uninterrupted during a future international crisis.

The Ukraine conflict has already demonstrated how satellite connectivity can become intertwined with military operations and geopolitical decisions. If access can be restricted because of a battlefield decision today, there is no guarantee that geopolitical pressure could not influence access tomorrow.

India therefore needs sovereign redundancy.

That means developing powerful domestic satellite constellations, secure satellite communications, indigenous ground infrastructure and the technological capability to operate independently when necessary.

The detention of journalists covering the October 10–11 protests in Delhi raises serious questions about press freedom. The Committee to Protect Journalists reported at least 43 journalists detained across Delhi, Ahmedabad and Pune, including at least 39 in Delhi. It also documented reports of journalists being struck and phones being seized. The crackdown unfolded amid barricades, restricted Metro access and a mobile internet shutdown around the protest area, making it harder for people to witness and document events. India ranked 157th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index. When reporters are prevented from filming, questioning officials,  or speaking to detained protesters, the public loses an important window into how power is exercised.

IFF condemns journalist’s detention and the seizure of their phones during the Delhi protests

New Delhi, 12 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the detention of journalists and the seizure of their' phones by the Delhi Police during the protests of 10 and 11 October 2026. The protests, sought the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. According to a report in Newslaundry, the police took three official phones from its reporters and an intern on 10 October. BOOM lost contact with its reporter Jagriti Trisha after her phone was taken, and Indian Express Hindi said its journalist Siya's phone was snatched on 11 October. Scroll's Shoaib Daniyal says he was pressured to delete videos he recorded inside a police bus.

Section 106 of the BNSS allows the police to seize property only in connection with a suspected offence, and Section 105 requires every seizure to be video recorded and the recording sent to a Magistrate. No provision, seizure memo or recording has been made public, and it is not known whether the phones were unlocked or their data copied. A reporter's phone holds unpublished material, private messages and the identities of sources. Under K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, any intrusion into privacy must be backed by law, necessary and proportionate. Making a journalist delete footage of police action destroys the record of how the police used their powers.

Further, on 5 October, the Delhi Police issued "Guidelines for journalists" asking reporters to carry identity cards issued by their organisations "and/or valid PIB/DIP accreditation cards". On 10 October, Newslaundry reported that police were asking media personnel whether they were YouTubers, refusing entry to those who were, and asking for PIB accreditation. Press cards however did not prevent detention and reporters from at least nine outlets were detained on 10 October, and from at least seven on 11 October. Digital journalist Pragya Mishra was detained in the RK Ashram area, and by her account her camera person was beaten even though both carried identification.

Detentions and the use of force are not ordinarily part of IFF's work given our focus on digital rights. We address them here because they affect the freedom of speech and expression of digital first journalists, who report and publish through their phones. Here we note, Article 19(1)(a) protects the freedom of the press (Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1985) 1 SCC 641), whether a journalist works for a newspaper or runs a YouTube channel. PIB accreditation has never been a condition for reporting from a public place. When the police check accreditation at a protest and detain those without it, they are illegally deciding who may report.

We note that on 11 October, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana of the Supreme Court heard a contempt petition alleging violation of the Court's order of 9 October on metro and train services, and a habeas corpus petition concerning the reported detention of about 7,000 people. The Court found a prima facie case and issued notice. Taking note of the Solicitor General's statement that internet services had been restored, it directed that that "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever." However, to our regret, there has been little compliance of this order as journalists were detained again that afternoon, a few hours after the order.
Our demands

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Delhi Police to:

1) Return every phone taken from journalists, disclose the legal basis, seizure memo and Section 105 recording for each, and confirm whether any data was copied.
2) Instruct all personnel in writing that no one may be made to delete footage or stopped from recording police action, and preserve all body-camera footage.
3) Withdraw the advisory of 5 October to the extent that it makes accreditation a condition for reporting, and ensure that journalists and creators covering protests are not detained or obstructed.
4) Place before the Supreme Court on 13 October 2026 the names of all journalists detained, the grounds of detention and the time of release. We also support the press bodies' call for an inquiry, which should be independent, time-bound and cover the complaints made by women journalists.
5) IFF will track compliance before the hearing on 13 October 2026 and is examining legal remedies, including for the phones taken from journalists. 

Journalists and creators who were detained, had devices taken, were made to delete footage, or had posts or accounts restricted for covering the protests may write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Blocking TIP’s X accounts is a new form of banning a political party: Irfan Degirmenci

n an interview with The Amargi, Irfan Degirmenci, a member of the Workers’ Party of Turkey (TIP) Party Assembly, discussed access restrictions targeting the party’s X accounts, the legal decision concerning his own account, and the broader crackdown on political opposition, and LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey.

He calls for solidarity among groups facing censorship and says political struggle must continue beyond social media platforms.

The Amargi: TIP recently announced that access restriction decisions had been issued against the party’s headquarters and Istanbul provincial organization accounts on X. The party stated that it believes the decisions are connected to its statements and broadcasts exposing alleged corruption involving a fund. Why do you think this is happening now?

Irfan Degirmenci: I am not sure whether the account of any political party in Turkey has been blocked in this way before. It is almost like the closure of a political party.

Twenty years ago, they would physically seal the entrance to a party’s headquarters and remove people from the building in handcuffs. In the digital age, there is no need to do that anymore. If you can obtain a court order without respecting universal legal principles, you can act without even notifying the person or institution concerned.

They saw how effectively TIP could organize through social media and how seriously the party was pursuing one of the biggest corruption scandals in the country’s recent history. Initially, the government seemed uncertain about how to respond. Then it quickly took action.

The public was led to believe that those who had made billions through the fund would be held accountable. That expectation lasted two or three days before those who should have been held responsible began to escape accountability. Meanwhile, journalists reporting on the allegations have faced pressure, and some have been detained.

I believe TIP has become a target partly because it has pursued these allegations effectively. I also believe the publication, on our X account, of a video alleging Justice Minister Akin Gurlek’s responsibility in these developments played a role in the decision against our party’s accounts.

The Amargi: What will TIP do if the access restriction decisions are implemented?

Irfan Degirmenci: We have no intention of behaving as though everything is normal. If we simply said we rejected the decision and would pursue a legal challenge, we would be practicing the conventional opposition politics that already exists in Turkey.

We intend to make them regret closing our accounts. We will continue to be present in the streets and public squares. We have a strong culture of protest, and wherever those responsible go, we will continue asking what happened to the money taken from the funds.

We always have a Plan B and a Plan C. We have many methods of struggle, including those used in the 1970s [printing leaflets, selling street newspapers, and using traditional methods of political organizing]. This is also a struggle that extends beyond Turkey: as peoples, we must consider what we can do against the alliance between international capital and autocratic leaders.

We also have a digital strategy. People can follow the party’s activities, find out where protests are taking place, and stay informed about current developments on our TIP mobile application. We will continue creating alternative ways to communicate and organize.

The Amargi: Your own X account has also been subject to an access restriction decision. What is the current situation?

Irfan Degirmenci: I have not received any decision by email from X or directly from a court. I learned about it through news reports. A journalist colleague sent me a copy of the court decision and asked whether I knew about it. I did not.

The decision concerns approximately 200 accounts, issued by a court in Bakirkoy, Istanbul. According to the information I received, four journalists have been treated differently within that group: the decision indicates that even if we change our usernames, we will still be unable to access the platform through our existing user IDs.

They want to erase me from public life. It feels as though they are saying, “We can do this to you whenever we want.” They want to keep us away from social platforms and silence us.

The restriction has not yet been implemented against my account. I have not received direct notification, and I am still astonished by the situation.

The Amargi: If your account is eventually blocked, will you move to another platform, such as Bluesky?

Irfan Degirmenci: Our fundamental contradiction is that we continue to communicate through X, a platform owned by Elon Musk, while criticizing the support wealthy business figures provide to autocratic governments.

Unfortunately, X remains the most widely used platform, which makes it difficult to leave. A boycott could be effective, and we will try to organize one in Turkey. We need a new platform that people can collectively move to and recognize as their new address.

People keep calling for a move to Bluesky, yet they continue posting on X to maintain their reach. The peoples of the world have not yet succeeded in acting collectively in this regard.

Personally, I am 50 years old, but I still try to adapt to new technologies. Because they want to make me invisible, I am trying to become even more visible. I have resumed my YouTube broadcasts, am trying to increase my Instagram following, and plan to start broadcasting on TikTok soon. There is no shortage of ways to continue. The methods of struggle do not run out.

The Amargi: These restrictions are not limited to politicians and journalists. LGBTQ+ organizations and activists have also faced access restrictions, alongside pressure on human rights organizations. Do you see these developments as part of a broader intervention in social life?

Irfan Degirmenci: Absolutely. There seems to be no clear limit to how far this can go. Those organizing against this darkness must learn to act together, setting aside their differences.

An attempt is being made to impose a single model of life on society. A rigid and conservative understanding of morality is being imposed and used to maintain political power. Yet the ruling order itself has no genuine moral principles. If you want to judge morality, look not between people’s legs, but inside bank vaults.

We have heard arguments about protecting families from an alleged “international LGBTQ+ lobby.” But what they call the “LGBTQ+ lobby” consists of civil society organizations coming together to defend fundamental human rights, including organizations in Turkey.

We are talking about a government and intelligence apparatus capable of sending police to the doors of civil society organizations even when they hold closed meetings. During Pride months in June, we have had to share the routes of planned marches on paper rather than openly, because we do not know who might be listening.

The Amargi: Political opposition movements and LGBTQ+ communities already struggle to find adequate representation in mainstream media. How does restricting their social media accounts affect their ability to communicate and organize?

Irfan Degirmenci: These groups are often portrayed as enemies, even when they appear in mainstream media. Social media has therefore become an important space for them to communicate and make themselves visible. When these accounts are blocked, it becomes much harder for these people and organizations to reach the public.

We can see similar patterns elsewhere. In the United States, as the Trump administration has faced difficulties over foreign policy, including the war involving Iran, the government has increasingly targeted transgender Americans. Turkey is not entirely different in this respect. When the government finds itself in difficulty, it brings another issue to the forefront.

The Amargi: What kind of solidarity is necessary between political opposition movements, LGBTQ+ communities and other groups facing restrictions?

Irfan Degirmenci: We must recognize that these different forms of repression are connected. Those confronting them cannot afford to remain isolated from one another. The people who want to impose a single way of life on society benefit when different groups remain divided.

We must continue finding ways to organize, communicate and support one another, even when the methods available to us change. If one of us is facing difficulties, we must be there to support them.

France: pre-insurrectional conflagration (surprised?)
----

1 France

The thugs, looters, black blocs, vandals and idiots who parasitized the processions of protesters, high-school students, trade unionists, ordinary impoverished people and left-wing bourgeois on Saturday in France put on an exceptional “performance” that has left the country stunned and the foreign press appalled. The scenes of insurrection, sometimes to the cry of “Revolution,” appeared more intense than the 2023 riots known as the Nahel riots (even though at the time 95 departments and hundreds of communes were affected, around 50,000 rioters, 12,000 vehicles burned, 2,500 buildings damaged or burned, thousands of arrests and detentions) and also than the action days of the Yellow Vests in 2018-2019.

In the streets of Paris as well as in those of the country’s main cities, hundreds of institutions and businesses were targeted, leaving entire streets littered with debris and the carcasses of burned two-wheelers in city centers. In Marseille, Lille, Angers and Bordeaux, protesters broke into town halls or prefectures to vandalize them. In Lyon, a tourist office branch was set on fire. In Limoges, the 19th-century Town Hall was “largely lost” to the https://t.co/VlxEwBkLZR the capital, “entire streets were methodically ravaged,” according to Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire (PS). Together with his counterparts from Lyon and Marseille, he asked to be received early next week by Prime Minister Sébastien https://t.co/YiYVFRHjIT total, 1,200 people were arrested on Saturday and 150 police officers and gendarmes were injured, according to the executive. Several protesters were also injured, some seriously, notably in Saint-Étienne, where a 17-year-old had his hand torn off by a police grenade.

----

2 Ukraine

Marco Rubio tried on Saturday evening to downplay Donald Trump’s decision to exempt Russia from new sanctions, insisting it was a 60-day pause aimed “sort of at ‘analyzing’ their economic repercussions.” Marco, Canard Hirsute likes you since you’re the only adult in the White House, but this is what’s called backpedaling in the semolina. A few hours earlier, Republican figures, in addition to Democrats, had attacked Donald Trump’s decision not to apply the so-called “Graham” law, named after a senator close to him who unfortunately died this summer. “It’s completely irresponsible,” denounced Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent critic of the American president on diplomatic issues. This exemption is a “mistake,” judged Ted Cruz, another influential Republican senator. 

“Trump has just given Putin his best birthday present,” underlined the leading Democratic voice in the Senate, Chuck Schumer. Donald Trump’s decision to exempt Russia from major new sanctions is an “encouragement” for Vladimir Putin, Volodymyr Zelensky denounced on Saturday, while Moscow for its part welcomed a “historic moment.”The Ukrainian president stated that the decision came on the very day Russia struck 15 important electrical infrastructures across Ukraine, in one of the “largest” attacks against the country’s energy network.

------

3 Israel

Masked Jewish settlers attacked Palestinians, representatives of the Catholic Church and European officials — the Belgian consul general, French and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor — in the occupied West Bank, in a village mainly populated by Christian Palestinians (yes, that exists). 

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar condemned the attack, which he attributed to “Israeli rioters.” The attack came the day after settlers assaulted American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was covering the olive harvest for the Washington Post.

--------------
4 India

Nobody in Europe gives a damn because it’s far away, but the protests in India concern respect for the rule of law and democracy in the most populous country on the planet. The leader of the “cockroaches” party, a youth movement born in the spring, was released on Saturday. 

The day after his arrest ahead of a demonstration in New Delhi against the revision of electoral rolls — which his movement considers favorable to the ultra-nationalist Hindu Prime Minister Narendra Modi — the founder of the Cockroach People’s Party (CJP), Abhijeet Dipke, 31, walked out of a police station on Saturday afternoon. Two other CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, remain in detention.The electoral reform, launched last year to remove duplicates, the deceased and fraudsters from the electoral lists, has, according to counts published in the media and by the opposition, struck off 130 million registered voters.

---------

5 Albania

Clashes continued on Saturday for the fifth day in Tirana, where protesters are demanding the resignation of the head of the Albanian socialist government and denouncing teaching conditions and university tuition rights. Protesters threw stones at the police and set fire to trash bins. In the evening, fires were started in several buildings, including the Supreme Court and the entrance of the Bank of Albania. 

The Ministry of Health indicated that 35 people were injured on Saturday, including 18 members of the security forces and 17 protesters.For the first time since these gatherings began, the police used rubber bullets. Prime Minister Edi Rama denounced the presence of “foreign hands” behind this wave of protest.

---

6. Iran / Saudi Arabia

Riyadh on Sunday acknowledged for the first time the combat death against the Houthis (Iran’s allies) of two soldiers, pilots of a helicopter shot down in Yemen.Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi declared for his part that his country stood ready to defend the kingdom if it “requested it,” specifying that any Egyptian deployment would require Parliament’s approval. text:
Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

Cyberattack
⚠️ An "E-statement" .exe from a trusted contact installed ManageEngine Endpoint Central (real IT software!) pointed at an attacker's server. They controlled my PC behind a black screen for 5 days. A statement is never an .exe. Verify before opening. #CyberSecurity

Details:
⚠️ My laptop was remotely controlled for 5 days in short bursts of time, and the tool they used was legitimate IT software.

Last week a known contact sent me an "E-statement" file. I opened it. Nothing seemed to happen.

Over the next few days my screen would suddenly go BLACK, the mouse moved by itself, and when the screen came back after a minute my programs had been closed. Someone was operating my computer behind a black screen. Only this happened, nothing else. This pattern continued for 2 days, and I started to dig.

What we found:
🔹 The file was a zip → a .vhd disk image → "E-statement（1).exe". Look closely: that "（" is a special Unicode bracket, used to fool filters.
🔹 It was digitally signed with a real (but expired, likely stolen) company certificate, so Windows showed it as "verified".
🔹 It silently installed @manageengine  Endpoint Central, a legitimate IT-management tool used by companies, connected to the attacker's own server. Antivirus didn't flag it, because it's real software.
🔹 The attacker used its remote-control "privacy mode" to blank my screen while they worked, including in the middle of the night once.
🔹 The agent protected itself: uninstalling asked for a code I didn't have, and its driver blocked deletion. I had to remove it in Safe Mode.

👉 Lessons:
1. "Sent by someone I trust" ≠ safe. Their account may be hacked. Confirm by phone first.
2. A bank statement is a PDF, never an .exe, .vhd, .iso or .zip with a program inside.
3. "Verified publisher" does not mean safe.
4. Black screen + mouse moving on its own = someone is remotely controlling your PC. Disconnect the internet immediately.
5. Check Settings → Apps for remote tools you didn't install: ManageEngine/Zoho UEMS, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, UltraViewer, RustDesk, ScreenConnect, etc.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

At the suggestion of @price_dominie I’m going to share a story about cops. I don’t love them or hate them as a whole; I have family that’s retired LE, close friends who are currently LE, and I even wore a badge for a brief stint over 25 years ago. 

15 years ago in December, I’d been hosting a guys night in my garage where everything was good up u til one guy started in about aliens. Most left when that started, but I decided to hang with him anyway and we ended up going out for a couple more beers. 

He dropped me back off after midnight, then put the pedal to the metal down my street. I started walking around my garage to head in for the night when I heard what sounded loud me a shotgun blast down the street. 

I immediately ran down the street to find out what kind of shenanigans were happening. As I got near the intersection at the other end of my block, I saw my friend wandering concussed, and another vehicle sitting in the ditch. His truck was about 20 feet off the road, I side someone’s yard, smashed into a tree. 

After trying to reason with him, I moved on to the unknown vehicle. The driver was not in the vehicle, a passenger was in the front seat bleeding profusely from his head, and a third was crunched up between the back hatch and the back seat and screaming. 

I pull off my shirt to make a pressure bandage for the front passenger and get it applied just as the first cop shows up. The cops first words “were you driving?” I tell him “no, I’m here giving first aid, you need to find the driver.” He runs around like a chicken with his head cut off as I make my way to the rear of the vehicle to check out and remove the rear passenger. 

Again, he comes and asked me if I’m the driver, in a more accusatory manner. Again, I tell him “no, I’m the only person here who isn’t injured.

A mi Ute or 2 passes again, before he accuses me of driving, and begins to attack me. I braced myself on his shoulders to maintain balance, as he pushed me up onto the street. At this time, a second officer arrives and makes me ride the lightning. 

When I regained control of my body, laying on the ground, I I tell him he’s got the wrong guy. He responds by telling me “I’m a cop and I can do whatever I want to do.” Next thing you know, I’m getting kneed in the head by them while they remove the probes. 

Shortly thereafter, they cuff me and carry me in a double chicken wing before looking at eachother and dropping me on my face in front of the patrol car camera. 

I get placed in the back of the patrol car, and a few minutes later, a much more rational officer comes and sits in the front seat to take statements. I tell him they need to find the driver, as I wasn’t driving. He immediately gets out of the vehicle and gets the other first responders in scene to canvass the area. Needless to say, they found the driver. Ejected from, and pinned under his own vehicle. 

It’s at this point the first 2 realize they fucked up and go into full crooked-cop mode. The third officer takes me back to the station where I spend a while giving him a full statement of what happened. They charged me with “Obstructing a Peace Officer,” and “Battery,” hoping they’d beat me into submission. 

The following Monday, I went to the PD and filed a FOIA request for all camera footage. They tried to claim it was damaged, I offered to bring in a forensics expert to recover it… About a week later, they provided the footage. 

I took the charges to jury trial. It was a 3 day shit-show. Rookie prosecutor, cops contradicting themselves on the stand, and one of them losing his temper and screaming in court. Needless to say, that jury took about 15 minutes from start to finish to find me not guilty.

Around this time, I contact a local reporter and provide him the video footage from the police cars. Through all this time, I’d learned that the first officer on scene had quite a past. He’d been fired from a neighboring department for beating restrained youths, and more.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
The Supreme Court has directed that the internet “should function unhindered” in Delhi. The government and the police must obey.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) notes the order passed today by the Supreme Court of India (Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana) in Shailendra Mani Tripathi v. Govind Mohan, Contempt Petition (Civil) Diary No. 63801/2026, heard with a connected habeas corpus petition. Assembling for an urgent hearing on a Sunday, the Court recorded that the petitioners had made out “a prima facie case”, issued notice to the alleged contemnors, and called for a counter affidavit and compliance report by 13 October 2026. 

At paragraph 16(c), it directed: “Internet facilities should function unhindered.” Unlike the directions on transport and movement, this one carries no qualification. The Court also directed that there shall be no illegal detention, and that lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in their work. While this direction is welcome, it should never have been necessary and does not extend to the reported and continuing instances of police violence. 

Mobile internet was reportedly suspended for twenty-four hours across a four-kilometre radius in central Delhi from 10 pm on 9 October, and counsel told the Court that about 7,000 people had been illegally detained in the city. The Union’s submission in Court was an oral assurance that internet facilities “have since been restored”. However such restoration after the fact is not accountability as under Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, a suspension order has to be published, must record its reasons, and must be proportionate and limited in duration. This was not done for the internet suspension in Delhi this week. 

IFF condemns a state of affairs in which it takes an urgent sitting of the Supreme Court and a contempt petition for the executive to be told that the internet in the national capital must stay on. We also note that  this order is only as good as its observance. Even after it was passed, we continue to notice instances in which the safety of protesters has been breached which throws into doubt whether the Union Government and the Delhi Police are observing the Court’s directions. Under Article 144 of the Constitution, all authorities, civil and judicial, are bound to act in aid of the Supreme Court.

We call upon the Union Government and the Delhi Police to:

1. Obey the Court’s directions in letter and spirit, and keep internet services in Delhi running without suspension, throttling or jamming.

2. Publish every order by which internet services were suspended in Delhi on 9 and 10 October 2026, with the reasons recorded and the findings of the Review Committee.

3. Ensure the safety of protesters, end illegal detentions, and let journalists and lawyers do their work.

4. Most importantly, respect the Constitution. The freedoms of speech and peaceful assembly under Article 19 and the guarantee of personal liberty under Article 21 are owed to every person in Delhi, including those who protest.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. STORY | Delhi Police gets 300 social media posts taken down for spreading 'rumours'

Delhi Police is monitoring various social media platforms to curb the spread of misinformation amid protests in the capital, with around 300 posts allegedly aimed at spreading rumours or creating public unrest taken down, police sources said on Monday.

The action comes days after police arrested a 24-year-old man for allegedly using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to create and circulate a fabricated video depicting a police officer sexually harassing a woman journalist during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The accused, identified as Nadeem Ahmed, allegedly circulated the video falsely portraying police personnel in an objectionable manner, police said. The incident is being investigated separately from the allegations of sexual harassment levelled against police personnel by women journalists.

The police have also approached social media platform X seeking the removal of objectionable and allegedly misleading content linked to the protests, sources said.

The .IN Registry took https://t.co/6D4RZacQWP off the internet three days after it went live, without notice or reasons. The site was a fully sourced, non-commercial record of the NEET paper-leak protests and the “Chalo Sansad” march. On 14 October 2026, the Delhi High Court issued notice in Sriram Viswanathan v. National Internet Exchange of India & Ors. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/IObo9F6mNB

Indian law already prescribes how online content may be blocked. Section 69A of the IT Act and the 2009 Blocking Rules require a written order, reasons, committee review and a hearing. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in Shreya Singhal (2015) because of these safeguards, and none were followed here. NIXI now says it will examine every .IN domain using “Sansad” or “Parliament”, acting on a private legal opinion and without any statutory power. (6/7)

Counsel for NIXI, MeitY, the Department of Consumer Affairs and GoDaddy appeared before Justice Amit Mahajan, and the matter will next be heard on 27 January 2027. The petition seeks restoration of the domain and disclosure of the legal opinion. It also asks that NIXI give prior notice, reasons and a hearing before suspending any .IN domain. If your .IN domain has been suspended without notice or reasons, write to us. (7/7)
